The WHO recommendations on child health are part of a series that also includes guidelines on newborn, maternal, and adolescent health. This document compiles WHO recommendations on child health to provide easy access for WHO staff, policymakers, program managers, and health professionals. It also aims to identify gaps for prioritizing guideline updates. The document addresses questions such as what health interventions a child should receive and when, as well as what health behaviors a caregiver should practice or avoid. WHO develops guidelines based on the highest international standards, emphasizing transparency and minimizing bias. The process, documented in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development, involves synthesizing and assessing evidence quality using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. Evidence quality is categorized as high, moderate, low, or very low, with corresponding levels of confidence in the effect estimates. An expert group formulates recommendations using a structured evidence-to-decision framework, considering the balance of benefits and harms, values and preferences of affected individuals, stakeholder perceptions, resource implications, the importance of the problem, and equity and human rights considerations. Recommendations are classified as strong or conditional. Strong recommendations indicate that the desirable effects outweigh the undesirable effects, while conditional recommendations reflect less certainty about the balance of benefits and harms. The quality of evidence, strength of recommendations, and links to sources are included in the publication. Different expert groups may use varying terminology, and readers are encouraged to refer to the source for more details. Publications are marked as New if published after 2013 or Update if revised since 2013. For immunization, WHO recommends a single dose of Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine for all infants in countries with a high burden of tuberculosis (TB), administered as soon as possible after birth. BCG vaccination is generally safe, even for asymptomatic HIV-positive infants, but should not be given to those with symptomatic HIV or other immunodeficiency states. In low TB burden countries, BCG vaccination may be limited to high-risk groups or replaced by intensified case detection and early treatment. The primary series of diphtheria-containing vaccines (DTwP or DTaP) should be administered in three doses starting at six weeks of age, with a minimum interval of four weeks. Additional doses may be given where resources allow. WHO also recommends the inclusion of conjugate Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) vaccines in all infant immunization programs as part of a comprehensive strategy to control pneumonia. Hib immunization schedules may include three primary doses without a booster, two primary doses plus a booster, or three primary doses with a booster. Immunization should start at six weeks of age, with intervals of at least four weeks between doses. Booster doses should be given at least six months after the primary series. Hib vaccine is not required for healthy children over five years of age. WHO recommends integrating hepatitis A vaccination into national immunization schedules for children aged one year or older in areas with intermediate endemicity or based on cost-effectiveness. All infants should receive their first dose of hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, preferably within 24 hours. Influenza vaccination is recommended for children aged 6–23 months in areas with sufficient resources and high disease burden. Measles vaccines should be administered to all susceptible children and adults without contraindications. The first dose should be given on time, with a second dose provided through routine services or mass campaigns. Measles elimination requires ≥95% nationwide coverage with both doses. In high-transmission areas, the first dose should be given at nine months of age, while in low-transmission areas, administration at 12 months is preferable. Countries with moderate to weak health systems may use regular measles immunization campaigns to protect children without access to routine services.
